cues.text: Today, a meme often means a captioned image or video that people copy and change online.

To understand why ideas go viral, we can start with *The Selfish Gene* (1976), where Richard Dawkins proposed “meme” as a name for a unit of cultural transmission: an idea, tune, fashion, or practice that passes from person to person.
His comparison with genes was powerful because it directed attention towards copying and survival.
However, cultural information is not literally DNA.
People can misunderstand it, combine it with other ideas, or deliberately redesign it.
Modern cultural-evolution research therefore treats the gene comparison as a useful starting point, not a complete explanation of culture.
Cultural evolution can be described through three linked processes.
**Transmission** happens when information moves between people through speech, imitation, writing, teaching, or media.
**Variation** appears when the information changes, either by accident or by design.
**Selection** happens when some versions are copied or remembered more than others.
Here, “selected” does not mean morally good, factually true, or biologically superior.
It only means that one version became more common or lasted longer in a particular environment.
A joke may become shorter because short versions are easier to retell.
A recipe may become more detailed because accuracy matters to the cooks using it.
Human goals shape each step.
Copying is not random.
People may notice content because it is surprising, useful, frightening, funny, or easy to remember.
They may also copy a person who seems respected or successful.
In one narrative experiment, both the content of a story and the supposed prestige of its source influenced transmission; prestige mattered, but several content effects were stronger.
Social information can then create a feedback loop.
In a controlled online music experiment, 14,341 people chose songs by unknown bands.
When participants could see earlier download numbers, popular songs became more unequal and final rankings became less predictable.
Quality still had some influence, but early popularity helped create later popularity.
A transmission test asks, “Will people pass this on?”
A truth test asks, “Is the claim supported by reliable evidence?”
These tests can produce different answers.
A large study followed about 126,000 stories shared on Twitter from 2006 to 2017 and used six fact-checking organizations to classify them.
In that dataset, false stories travelled farther, faster, deeper, and more broadly than true stories.
The researchers also found that false news tended to be more novel.
This does not prove that every false claim beats every true one, or that the same pattern exists on every platform.
It shows why share counts cannot replace evidence.
People often use “viral” to mean “very popular,” but network scientists can ask a more precise question: what shape did the spread take?
Imagine two messages with one million views.
A celebrity sends the first directly to a huge audience, creating a broadcast shaped like a star.
The second passes through many generations: one person shares it, several recipients share it again, and new branches continue.
Researchers call this second quality **structural virality**.
After examining one billion diffusion events on Twitter, they found that popular events had many different shapes.
However, structural virality was usually low, and a large broadcast often produced most of the popularity.
Reach and person-to-person depth are not the same measurement.
The language of contagion is another model, not a claim that ideas are diseases.
In a **simple contagion**, one contact may be enough to transmit information, as when you learn that a concert exists.
A **complex contagion** requires reinforcement from several people before someone adopts a risky, costly, or uncertain behavior.
Joining a protest, using an unfamiliar technology, or accepting a new group rule may work this way.
In a randomized online experiment with 1,528 participants, a health behavior spread farther and faster through clustered networks than through random networks.
Repeated social signals helped adoption.
The result does not mean clustering always wins; it shows that the kind of decision changes which network structure is useful.
A network is a pattern of connections between people or groups.
Dense clusters create repeated contact, shared expectations, and trust, so they can support complex adoption.
Bridges connect different clusters and carry information into new communities.
Yet one weak bridge may deliver a message without providing enough reinforcement for action.
Complex-contagion theory therefore highlights bridge **width**: several independent links between groups may matter more than one long connection.
There is no universally perfect network.
Tight clusters can strengthen support but also trap an idea inside one group.
Numerous bridges can increase reach but may weaken repeated confirmation.
The outcome depends on what is spreading and what adoption requires.
People cannot inspect every message they receive.
In one agent-based model, limited attention and network structure produced large differences in meme popularity even when the modeled items had equal quality.
This does not prove that real ideas are equal; it reveals how competition for attention can magnify small accidents.
Platforms add another layer by ranking what users see.
A large randomized Twitter experiment found that an algorithmic timeline changed the relative visibility of political content compared with a reverse-chronological feed.
Content matters too: in selected political discussions, moral-emotional language was associated with more sharing, especially inside ideological groups.
That finding was observational, so it is not a universal recipe.
Algorithms, human choices, and content interact in feedback loops.
No single feature explains why an idea takes over.
A better analysis uses six layers.
**Content** asks what the message says and how memorable it is.
**Mind** asks what emotions, knowledge, and goals people bring.
**Source** asks who communicates it and what social signals surround that person.
**Network** asks how groups, clusters, and bridges are arranged.
**Time** asks whether events and early accidents create an opportunity.
**Platform** asks how interfaces and ranking distribute attention.
These layers can also guide responsible communication.
Make accurate information clear and easy to pass on, but keep the evidence attached.
Build trusted connections across groups, but do not manufacture false popularity.
The aim is not merely to win attention; it is to help valuable ideas travel without sacrificing truth.
